tytul: Wild garlic in soy sauce: why there is no recipe here
wstep: There is no recipe here for raw wild garlic leaves pickled in soy sauce, Korean style (myeongi namul). [T:-]

ostrzezenia.tekst: Almost any food that is not very acidic, with a pH above 4.6, can support the growth of Clostridium botulinum and toxin production. [T:SLO-023]
According to the FDA, the minimum temperature for growth and toxin production by Clostridium botulinum type E and nonproteolytic types B and F is 38°F (3.3°C). [T:MIE-059]
According to BfR, young wild garlic leaves resemble those of the poisonous lily of the valley and the very poisonous autumn crocus; when in doubt, it is better not to eat them. [T:SUS-337]

According to AGES, wild garlic leaves may be contaminated with fox tapeworm eggs, which can cause a life-threatening disease in humans; the eggs survive usual freezing at -18 °C and are killed at around +60 °C. [T:SUS-338]

akapity: All fresh vegetables except most tomatoes are low-acid foods with a pH above 4.6. [T:ACI-005]
This pickle uses soy sauce, not vinegar. [T:-]
The leaves in this pickle are raw, so they are not heated to the temperature at which, according to AGES, fox tapeworm eggs are killed. [T:SUS-338]
According to AGES, wild garlic is also confused with spotted arum, Solomon’s seal and wild tulips. [T:SUS-337]
JarAtlas rule: if you are not sure that every leaf is wild garlic, do not use the leaves. [T:SUS-337]
This pickle is meant to be kept in the refrigerator. [T:-]
JarAtlas has found no tested recipe for wild garlic in soy sauce from a checked source. [T:-]
